newsitem.title: USA: US 30-yr mortgage rate up to 8.18 pct in Apr 4 wk.
newsitem.headline: US 30-yr mortgage rate up to 8.18 pct in Apr 4 wk.

text.p: The average commitment rate on U.S. 30-year fixed rate mortgages shot up to 8.18 percent in the week ending April 4, the highest since a rate of 8.28 percent in the September 13, 1996 week, Freddie Mac said Thursday.
The widely expected rise above eight percent was the first for the 30-year since the October 4, 1996 week when it averaged 8.06 percent.

Fifteen-year fixed-rate mortgages also rose in the week to an average 7.70 percent, the highest since a rate of 7.81 percent in the September 13, 1996 week. Last week's 15-year rate averaged 7.48 percent, Freddie Mac said.

One-year adjustable rate mortgages inched upward to 5.80 percent in the week, the highest since they stood at 5.82 percent in the week ended September 27, 1996. Last week, the ARM averaged 5.71 percent.
A year ago, the 30-year rate averaged 7.78 percent, the 15-year 7.29 percent and the ARM 5.62 percent.

"This week's interest rates further reflect the rate hike by the Fed, but the survey also incorporates the reaction to the strong home sales figures," said Robert Van Order, Freddie Mac chief economist.
"The employment figures will be released tomorrow and that will certainly influence next week's survey results."
Last month, the Federal Reserve increased the federal funds rate by a quarter-percentage point, causing a rippling increase in interest rates.
The National Association of Realtors last week said U.S. February sales of existing homes rose nine percent to an annualized rate of 4.26 million units.
On Friday the Labor Department will issue U.S. employment data for March.

Lenders charged an average 1.7 percent in fees and points on both 30- and 15-year loans, down from 1.8 percent last week. They charged 1.4 percent on ARM loans, unchanged from last week. Freddie Mac is a corporation chartered by Congress that buys mortgages from lenders and packages them into securities for investors.
